title: If Your User Story Names a Dropdown, It's Not a User Story
description:
A user story captures a piece of functionality from the user's point of view, focused on why they want it, not a technical implementation spec. The moment it names a specific dropdown, table, or button, it has stopped being a user story and started locking in one solution. This Short shows the weak-versus-strong example straight from the lesson and the template that keeps you honest: as a type of user, I want to do some action, so that a benefit.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/product-manager-mastery-path/level-1/05-writing-requirements/

#Shorts

beats.narration: If your user story names a dropdown menu, it's not a user story anymore. It's an implementation spec wearing a costume.
Weak version: add a filter dropdown to the reports page. That's a UI element, not a need. The strong one names who wants it, and why.

display.code:
Weak:   "Add a filter dropdown to the reports page."

Strong: "As a team lead reviewing weekly reports,
         I want to filter results by team member,
         so that I can check one person's numbers
         without scanning the whole list."

beats.narration: A user story captures a need from the user's point of view, focused on why they want it, not how you build it.
This template keeps you honest. It leaves room for design and engineering to propose something better. Maybe a saved filter beats a dropdown entirely.

display.code:
As a [type of user],
I want to [do some action],
so that [benefit/outcome].

beats.narration: So name the user, the action, and the benefit. Let the team name the dropdown.
Full breakdown, plus how a PRD ties your stories together, in the lesson.
